title: Hephaestus
wiki_lead:
Hephaestus (UK:  hih-FEE-stəs, US:  hih-FES-təs; eight spellings; Ancient Greek: Ἥφαιστος, romanized: Hḗphaistos) is the Greek god of artisans, blacksmiths, carpenters, craftsmen, fire, metallurgy, metalworking, sculpture, and volcanoes. In Greek mythology, Hephaestus was the son of Hera, either on her own or by her husband Zeus. He was cast off Mount Olympus by his mother Hera because of his lameness, the result of a congenital impairment, or in another account, by Zeus for protecting Hera from his advances.
As a smithing god, Hephaestus created all the weapons of the gods in Olympus. He served as the blacksmith of the gods, and was worshipped in the manufacturing and industrial centres of Greece, particularly Athens. The cult of Hephaestus was based in Lemnos. Hephaestus's symbols are a smith's hammer, anvil, and a pair of tongs. In Rome, he was equated with Vulcan.

As a smithing god, Hephaestus created all the weapons of the gods in Olympus. He served as the blacksmith of the gods, and was worshipped in the manufacturing and industrial centres of Greece, particularly Athens. The cult of Hephaestus was based in Lemnos. Hephaestus's symbols are a smith's hammer, anvil, and a pair of tongs. In Rome, he was equated with Vulcan.


Etymology
Hephaestus is probably associated with the Linear B (Mycenaean Greek) inscription 𐀀𐀞𐀂𐀴𐀍, A-pa-i-ti-jo, found at Knossos. The inscription indirectly attests his worship at that time because it is believed that it reads the theophoric name (H)āpʰaistios, or Hāphaistion. The Greek theonym Hēphaistos is most likely of Pre-Greek origin, as the form without -i- (Attic Hēphastos) shows a typical Pre-Greek variation and points to an original sy.


Epithets
The epithets by which Hephaestus is known by the poets generally allude to his skill in the plastic arts or to his figure or disability. The Greeks frequently placed miniature statues of Hephaestus near their hearths, and these figures are the oldest of all his representations. The meaning of some of his epithets are:

Amphigyḗeis often translated as "the lame one"; literally "lame on both sides" vel sim. (Ἀμφιγυήεις)
Kyllopodíōn "club-footed" or "of dragging feet" (Κυλλοποδίων)
Khalkeús "coppersmith" (Χαλκεύς)
Klytotékhnēs "renowned artificer" (Κλυτοτέχνης)
Polýmētis "shrewd, crafty" or "of many devices" (Πολύμητις)
Aitnaîos "Aetnaean" (Αἰτναῖος), owing to his workshop supposedly being located below Mount Aetna.
Polýphrōn "ingenious, inventive" (Πολύφρων)
Agaklytós "very famous, glorious" (Ἀγακλυτός)
Aithalóeis theós "sooty god" (Αἰθαλόεις θεός)


Mythology


Parentage
In Homer's Iliad, Hephaestus is described as the son of Hera; the Iliad seemingly also refers to Zeus as his father at two points, though it is possible these passages are not referring to Hephaestus as Zeus's literal son. The Odyssey does, however, refer explicitly to Hephaestus as having "two parents", the identity of whom would presumably be Zeus and Hera. In Hesiod's Theogony, Hera gives birth to Hephaestus on her own, out of revenge for Zeus having, without her, fathered Athena (the daughter of Zeus and Metis). Apollodorus similarly states that Hera gives birth to Hephaestus alone, though he also relates that, according to Homer, Hephaestus is one of the children of Zeus and Hera.

grok_lead: Hephaestus (Ancient Greek: á¼­ÏÎ±Î¹ÏÏÎ¿Ï, Há¸phaistos) was the ancient Greek god of fire, metalworking, forges, stonemasonry, sculpture, and craftsmanship, often depicted as a bearded, vigorous man wielding a hammer and tongs while working at his anvil. Unlike the idealized forms of other Olympian deities, Hephaestus was portrayed as physically lame and ungainly, a trait stemming from his birth or a fall from Olympus, which set him apart as the divine artisan whose ingenuity compensated for his appearance. His forge, located beneath volcanoes or within his self-built palace on Mount Olympus, symbolized the transformative power of fire in shaping metals and creating wondrous artifacts, linking him to both creation and destruction through volcanic activity. In Greek mythology, Hephaestus's parentage varied across accounts: Hesiod's Theogony describes him as the parthenogenetic offspring of Hera alone, conceived in anger after her rivalry with Zeus over Athena's birth, making him a rare self-generated child among the gods. Homer's Iliad, however, presents him as the legitimate son of both Zeus and Hera, emphasizing his integration into the Olympian family despite his disabilities. His lameness originated from being hurled from Olympus by Hera at birth due to his deformity, or alternatively by Zeus during a quarrel, after which he landed on the island of Lemnos and was raised by its nymphs or the Sintians. These myths highlight themes of rejection and resilience, with Hephaestus eventually returning to Olympus through his craftsmanship, such as by trapping Hera in a golden throne of his making to force his reinstatement. Hephaestus's role as the supreme divine smith is central to epic narratives, where he forges iconic items like the armor of Achilles, adorned with intricate scenes of war and cosmic order, as detailed in Homer's Iliad. He also crafted Pandora, the first woman, at Zeus 's command in Hesiod's accounts, endowing her with beauty and guile, and created automated golden handmaidens to assist him in his workshop. A prominent myth involves his marriage to Aphrodite, arranged by Zeus to resolve disputes among the gods, yet marred by her affair with Ares; Hephaestus cunningly trapped the lovers in an unbreakable net of his forging, exposing their infidelity to the Olympians in Homer's Odyssey. These stories underscore his cleverness and essential contributions to divine society, from building the palaces of Olympus to inventing tools that advanced godly and heroic endeavors. Cult worship of Hephaestus centered on sites tied to craftsmanship and fire, with major sanctuaries on the island of Lemnos âhis legendary birthplace and refugeâand in Athens, where the well-preserved Temple of Hephaestus (Hephaisteion) in the Agora, built around 450 BCE, served as a hub for festivals like the Apaturia and torch races honoring artisans. In Athens, he was paired with Athena as protectors of handicrafts, reflecting his patronage over blacksmiths, carpenters, and sculptors in daily life. His Roman counterpart, Vulcan, inherited similar attributes but emphasized fire's destructive aspects more prominently, with cults in volcanic regions like Sicily. Through these traditions, Hephaestus embodied the valorization of labor and technology in ancient Greek culture, influencing later artistic and literary depictions of the inventive underdog.
